finding.claim: Negative amount in /transfer lets an attacker take funds from another account

trace.note: amount read from request body with no sign check
balance check BAL[g.user] < amount passes for negative amount

finding.guards_checked: Balance comparison at line 11 (bypassed for negative amounts). No amount > 0 check, no type or range validation, no check that 'to' differs from or is a real account. /withdraw has amount <= 0 check but /transfer does not.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check on /transfer is the balance comparison at bank.py:11 (BAL[g.user] < amount), which a negative amount always passes. No sign or range check on amount, no validation of `to`, and no authentication code in the directory. The amount <= 0 guard exists only in /withdraw (bank.py:21), not /transfer.
verdict.reason: bank.py:10-14 reads an attacker-supplied amount and applies it without a sign check, so a negative amount passes the bank.py:11 balance check and moves funds from `to` into g.user (bank.py:13-14). The one caveat is that g.user is set outside this code (the directory contains only bank.py), so the attacker is assumed to be any authenticated user; that is the normal threat model for a transfer endpoint.

finding.claim: Check-then-act race on balance allows double-spend and overdraft in /withdraw and /transfer
finding.source: Concurrent POST requests from the same account to /withdraw or /transfer; Flask serves requests in parallel threads by default
finding.sink: Balance debit BAL[g.user] -= amount (bank.py:23 for withdraw, bank.py:13 for transfer)

trace.note: request A reads balance and passes the check
request B reads the same balance before A debits and also passes
both requests debit, so the balance goes negative or funds are spent twice

finding.guards_checked: Balance check at line 21 is not atomic with the debit. No lock, transaction, or per-account serialization in the file.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are the balance comparisons at bank.py:11 and bank.py:21, and they are not atomic with the debits at bank.py:13 and bank.py:23. No lock, transaction, or per-account serialization exists in bank.py (a grep for Lock, transaction, threaded, before_request finds nothing). Flask's default threaded serving is not overridden in this file.
verdict.reason: The check at bank.py:21 and the debit at bank.py:23 are separate steps with no lock, so two concurrent /withdraw requests from the same account can both pass the check and both debit (the same applies to bank.py:11 and bank.py:13 for /transfer), letting an account overdraw its own balance; the attacker only needs to be the account owner, a normal low-privilege role, and g.user is never assigned in the available code so the auth source is unverified, but that does not change the race.

finding.claim: NaN amount bypasses balance and positivity checks and corrupts balances, including the victim's on transfer
finding.source: request.json["amount"] (bank.py:20 and bank.py:10). Python json accepts the NaN literal by default and Flask request.json uses it.
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount (bank.py:23 and bank.py:13) and BAL[to] += amount (bank.py:14)

trace.note: NaN <= 0 is False and BAL[g.user] < NaN is False, so the abort is skipped
sender balance becomes NaN; later comparisons are always False so withdrawals are unlimited
via /transfer with to=victim and amount=NaN, the victim balance also becomes NaN, destroying their funds

finding.guards_checked: amount <= 0 check (bank.py:21) and balance comparison (bank.py:11 and bank.py:21). Neither rejects NaN because every comparison with NaN is False. No math.isfinite check.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. The only checks are `BAL[g.user] < amount` at bank.py:11 (transfer) and `amount <= 0 or BAL[g.user] < amount` at bank.py:21 (withdraw). Both are comparisons that evaluate False for NaN, so `abort(400)` at bank.py:12 and bank.py:22 is never reached. No math.isfinite or type check exists anywhere in bank.py, and bank.py is the only file in the directory.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: request.json["amount"] at bank.py:10/20 accepts a NaN literal (Python json.loads default), NaN passes the checks at bank.py:11 and bank.py:21 because every comparison with NaN is False, and bank.py:13/14/23 then write NaN into BAL, including the victim's balance via `to` at bank.py:14. The attacker only needs whatever authenticated identity sets g.user, which is not defined in this directory (no auth middleware present), so it is an ordinary user reaching a flaw that corrupts other accounts. Caveat: g.user's setup is outside the provided code, but that does not block the finding.

finding.claim: Transfer to an unknown recipient debits the sender then raises KeyError, destroying the sender's funds (non-atomic)
finding.sink: BAL[to] += amount (bank.py:14) after the debit at bank.py:13

trace.note: to read from request body with no existence check
to not in BAL, so KeyError is raised (HTTP 500) with no rollback

finding.guards_checked: No existence check on 'to'. No try/except or transactional rollback. Impact is limited to the attacker burning their own funds.

verdict.guard_found: none. bank.py:9 reads request.json["to"] with no existence check. bank.py:11 checks only the sender's balance, not the recipient. bank.py:13 debits BAL[g.user] before bank.py:14 reads BAL[to], which raises KeyError for an unknown recipient. There is no try/except or rollback, and BAL is a plain in-memory dict. Any authentication that sets g.user is defined outside this file, and I could not verify it here.
verdict.reason: The trace matches bank.py:9, 13, and 14: the sender is debited at line 13, then `BAL[to] += amount` at line 14 raises KeyError for an unknown `to` with no rollback, so the defect is real. Severity is low, though: the sender is g.user, so the only party who loses funds is the attacker, and the claim should be treated as a non-atomic correctness bug rather than a security vulnerability.

finding.source: Unknown. g.user is read at bank.py:11, 13, 21, 23 but never set in bank.py.
finding.sink: Every balance read and write keyed on g.user (bank.py:11, 13, 21, 23)

verdict.guard_found: none in bank.py: no auth decorator, before_request, or session check. The only file in the directory is bank.py, so nothing sets g.user here.
verdict.reason: The trace lines are accurate: bank.py:11, 13, 21 and 23 read or write BAL[g.user], and no line in bank.py assigns g.user, so whether a client can set it (and so impersonate any user) depends on code that is not in the directory.
